summary: This work demonstrates that distributed quantum error correction codes implemented over modular quantum networks can tolerate both scheduled node replacement and catastrophic unscheduled node failure, whereas monolithic systems hit a logical error rate floor from such events. For a per-round node failure probability of $p/100$, distributed toric codes outperform monolithic implementations below a physical error rate of 0.05%.
motivation: Scaling fault-tolerant quantum computers to utility-scale requires $10^5$–$10^6$ physical qubits, but monolithic scaling is engineering-intensive. Distributed QEC across modular quantum processing units offers an alternative, but device failures would be catastrophic in standard implementations—motivating a study of failure tolerance.
method: The authors analyze distributed implementations of toric and semi-hyperbolic Floquet codes ($[[576,20,12]]$ example) partitioned over QPUs with $16$–$48$ qubits each via spectral partitioning. For scheduled downtime, qubits are teleported transversally to replacement nodes; for unscheduled failure, failed nodes are replaced and their qubits initialized to maximally mixed states, treated as correlated errors correctable by standard syndrome-based decoding. Simulations use circuit-level noise with local errors at probability $p_l=p$ and non-local Bell state errors at $p_{nl}=10p$, with node failure modeled as per-round depolarization at $p_{dropout}=p/100$.
result: Scheduled swap-out has negligible impact on logical error rates for both code families. Under unscheduled failure at $p_{dropout}=10^{-4}$ per round, distributed toric codes achieve $P_L	imes100$ lower than monolithic systems; monolithic codes hit an analytical floor $P_L	hicksim 3	imes10^{-3}$ from equation $1-(1-p_{dropout})^r$, while distributed codes suppress both node failure and circuit noise through increasing code distance, with crossover at $p	hicksim 1.5	imes 10^{-4}$ for $d=6$ toric codes.
